near_miss.lead: kinship chains with *ph2ter-/*meh2ter- (Ir. mac athair do māthar; ON faðir Helgu móður Einars)
near_miss.why_not: genealogical listing; father/mother words co-occur in every genealogy, no shared figure

near_miss.lead: merism 'alive or dead' (MIr. a béo no a marb; béo nó marb ~ Skt amṛta-/jīvati)
near_miss.why_not: Irish is the everyday 'bring him dead or alive' formula of late Fenian prose; Skt passage is not a merism ('no evildoer lives while the husband is not dead'); 'living/dead' pairing is universal

near_miss.lead: binomial 'mother and father' (máthair ⁊ athair ~ πατρὸς καὶ μητέρος ~ matrem et patrem ~ pitṛ mātṛ)
near_miss.why_not: the pair is a natural binomial in every language; Irish contexts (Acallam, Patrick's curses/blessings, division of a fee into thirds) share no wording beyond the two nouns with the partners

near_miss.lead: weeping: déra co tróm ... tar a gruaidib ~ largus lacrumarum
near_miss.why_not: only dér ~ lacrima shared; trom ~ trudo is a root coincidence with no shared sense (Plautus 'be thrust out'); tears over cheeks is generic

near_miss.lead: full (lán) cup of water (uisce) / drink water (ól ... uisce ~ πίνω ὕδωρ)
near_miss.why_not: everyday vocabulary, no congruent context or figure

near_miss.lead: hounds (cú) pursue a hind (eilit) ~ κύων ἐλάφοιο δίηται
near_miss.why_not: real-world hunting scene; eilit and ἔλαφος are different derivatives of *h1el-; verbs not cognate; no evidence beyond co-reference

near_miss.lead: cú + míl ~ κύνες + μῆλα (míl ~ μῆλον is a good etymology)
near_miss.why_not: contexts diverge: Irish hound kills game animals, Homeric dogs guard flocks; no shared syntax beyond co-occurrence

near_miss.lead: inexpressibility topos: 'if there were seven tongues in my head ... I could not tell half or a third of it' (MIr. secht tengtha im cind) ~ Il. 2.489 οὐδ' εἴ μοι δέκα μὲν γλῶσσαι (recalled; Il. 2 is in the Homer corpus but not in this slab)
near_miss.why_not: attractive lead, but no partner passage in the slab carries it (Lucretius and AV partners are unrelated), so the anchoring rule cannot be met; also the many-tongues topos is a widely diffused literary commonplace (Vergil, Christian Latin) that could reach Irish via Latin

error.correct_reading: cuach 'cup, goblet' is a loan from Latin caucus; not from *káput (same lemma unmapped earlier in the line)
error.evidence: cuach is the cup of water named in the context line; no Celtic sound law gives cuach from *kaput-

error.correct_reading: thes = adverb tess/thess 'in the south' (Síd Liamna ... thes), not téit 'goes'
error.evidence: phrase 'ac Síd Liamna Lendchaime thes' names a place 'in the south'; cf. 'rig Laigen andes' in context

error.correct_reading: nema 'take' < *nem-; the negative particle *né is a spurious candidate
Caílte (name of Caílte mac Rónáin), not calad
error.evidence: speaker named Cáilte throughout the Acallam passage
